ghs-overview.title: GHS and the Hazard Communication Standard
ghs-overview.content: The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) is the international framework adopted by OSHA through the Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200. It standardizes how chemical hazards are classified, labeled, and communicated so workers anywhere can identify hazards and take appropriate precautions. GHS labeling applies to all hazardous chemicals in the workplace — on original containers and secondary containers.

product-supplier-id.title: Product Identifier and Supplier Information
product-supplier-id.content: Every GHS label must include a product identifier — the chemical name, code number, or batch number that allows the SDS to be located. The label must also include the supplier identifier: the name, address, and telephone number of the manufacturer, importer, or other responsible party. These two elements link the container to the chemical's complete hazard documentation and allow workers and emergency responders to quickly get more information.

ghs-pictograms.title: GHS Pictograms
ghs-pictograms.content: GHS pictograms are standardized graphic symbols enclosed in a red diamond frame. Each pictogram communicates a specific category of hazard: the flame for flammable materials, the skull and crossbones for acute toxicity, the corrosion symbol for substances that damage skin, eyes, or metals, the flame over circle for oxidizers, the gas cylinder for gases under pressure, the exclamation mark for irritants or less severe acute hazards, and others. Workers should be able to recognize each pictogram and understand the type of hazard it represents.

signal-words.title: Signal Words
signal-words.content: GHS labels use one of two signal words to indicate relative hazard severity. 'Danger' is used for the more severe hazard categories — conditions that present a higher risk of injury or death. 'Warning' is used for less severe categories. A signal word helps workers quickly assess the urgency of precautions. Some chemicals may not require a signal word if they do not meet classification criteria for those hazard categories.

hazard-statements.title: Hazard Statements
hazard-statements.content: Hazard statements describe the nature and degree of the chemical hazard. Examples include 'Flammable liquid and vapor,' 'Causes serious eye damage,' or 'May cause cancer.' Each statement is standardized and assigned a unique code (H-code) in the GHS system. Multiple hazard statements may appear on one label if the chemical has multiple hazards. Reading hazard statements helps workers understand exactly what risk they face when handling the chemical.

precautionary-statements.title: Precautionary Statements
precautionary-statements.content: Precautionary statements describe recommended measures to minimize or prevent adverse effects from chemical exposure or improper handling. They are organized into four categories: Prevention (actions to avoid exposure), Response (actions if exposure or emergency occurs), Storage (safe storage conditions), and Disposal (how to safely dispose of the chemical or container). Each statement is standardized with a P-code and must appear on the GHS label.

secondary-container-labeling.title: Secondary Container and Workplace Labeling
secondary-container-labeling.content: When a hazardous chemical is transferred from its original container into a secondary container — such as a spray bottle, bucket, or portable tank — the chemical hazard information must still be communicated. Workplace labels may use the full GHS label format or an alternative system that conveys the same hazard information. Unlabeled or unidentified containers must not be used. If a label is missing, damaged, or unreadable, the container should be set aside and reported, and use should stop until the hazard information is confirmed.
